pronunciation.approximation: Say "haumiatiketike" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Haumiatiketike".

kin.label: Māori form
kin.form: Haumia-tiketike — the hyphenated form of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855) and John White, Ancient History of the Māori

kin.label: Brother and counterpart
kin.form: Rongo(-māui), god of cultivated food — together the two brothers divide the vegetable world into what is planted and what is gathered (Orbell 1998)

kin.label: Parents
kin.form: Rangi, the sky-father, and Papa, the earth-mother — Haumia is one of their children in the Māori creation cycle

pronunciation.note: Haumia-tiketike is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Māori spelling writes the name without macrons, so no diacritic or distinctive letter is lost against plain ASCII — only the capital distinguishes the temple form. The hyphenated scholarly form Haumia-tiketike is traditional (Grey 1855; White), not a phonetic restoration.

domains.title: Haumiatiketike
domains.subtitle: Wild Food
domains.lead: Haumia-tiketike is the Māori god of uncultivated food — the bracken fernroot (aruhe) dug from the wild with a digging stick, the foil to his brother Rongo's planted kūmara. A child of Rangi and Papa, he hid within the earth-mother's body when the world was divided and never left it: wild food belongs to Papa herself, and cannot be owned, only gathered.

cards.name: Fernroot (Aruhe)
cards.desc: His plant: the bracken fern (Pteridium esculentum), whose starchy rhizomes were dug, beaten, washed, and steamed into a staple of pre-European Aotearoa.

cards.name: Child of Rangi and Papa
cards.desc: One of the children of the sky-father and earth-mother; brother of Tāne, Tangaroa, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, and Rongo (Grey, Polynesian Mythology ch. 1).

cards.name: Sheltered in the Earth
cards.desc: When his brother Tāne pried the parents apart, Haumia hid in Papa's bosom and stayed — the wild food that grows unseen within the mother.

cards.name: The Digging Stick (Kō)
cards.desc: The foot-driven spade of his harvest: fernroot was dug, never planted — the difference between Haumia's wild plenty and Rongo's cultivated gardens.

symbols.name: The bracken frond
symbols.meaning: Pteridium esculentum — the wild fern whose starchy rhizome fed the people when the kūmara crop failed

symbols.name: The digging stick (kō)
symbols.meaning: The foot-driven spade for unearthing fernroot — gathering rather than planting, the sign of uncultivated food

symbols.name: The earth-mother's bosom
symbols.meaning: Papa's body, where Haumia hid when the world was separated — wild food as the earth's own gift

symbols.name: The earth oven (hāngī, umu tī)
symbols.meaning: The steaming pit that leached and cooked the bitter fernroot into a staple — the 'fern oven' of tradition

symbols.name: The uncultivated ground
symbols.meaning: Fern country — the bracken clearings of the bush edge, territory no fence enclosed and no hand had sown

mythology.lead: Haumia-tiketike's stories are chapters of the Māori creation cycle: the separation of sky and earth, the war among the children, and the settlement of the food quest. His single decisive act is a refusal — to leave the earth-mother's body — and from that refusal the wild food of Aotearoa takes its sanctity.

myths.title: Child of the Sky and the Earth
myths.text: In the Māori creation cycle recorded by George Grey in Polynesian Mythology (1855) and in the fuller recensions of John White's Ancient History of the Māori, the sky-father Rangi and the earth-mother Papa lay locked in an embrace that left no room for light or life. Their children — Tāne, Tangaroa, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, Rongo-māui, Haumia-tiketike and the rest — grew cramped in the darkness between them. Among them Haumia was the quiet one, the god whose portion was to be everything the forest floor offered without planting. When at last the brothers voted on whether the parents should be separated, Haumia stood with Tāne: the world must be divided so that light, food, and people could come into it. The genealogy is short and absolute: every wild root dug in Aotearoa descends from this moment, when the children of the dark chose to break their parents' embrace and make room for a harvest.

myths.title: Hidden in the Earth-Mother
myths.text: Tāne thrust his parents apart, raising the sky on his shoulders and pressing the earth down, and the world took its shape. But the separation left some children with nowhere to go. Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, raged at what had been done and turned on his brothers; Tāne and Tangaroa fled to the forests and the sea. Rongo-māui took refuge inside the body of Papa, and Haumia-tiketike went with him — into the earth-mother's bosom, where the two brothers have remained ever since (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, 'The children of Heaven and Earth'). The story explains the Māori food world with an elegant symmetry: Rongo, who hid in the earth, is the god of the kūmara that must be planted; Haumia, who hid with him, is the god of the fernroot that is only gathered. What the mother shelters she does not surrender to the cultivator.

myths.title: The Food of the Conquered
myths.text: When Tāwhirimātea's storms failed to unmake the world, Tūmatauenga — the fierce brother of humankind — took revenge on all who had sided against him. One by one he hunted his brothers down: Tāne's birds, Tangaroa's fish and seals, the very forests and waves were made food for Tū and his children, which is why people eat them to this day. But two brothers escaped him. Rongo and Haumia had hidden so deep within the body of Papa that no attack could reach them, and so Tū declared his sentence over them instead: because they dared not face him, they would be dug up — unearthed with the digging stick as the food of the conquered (Grey, 'The war of the children'; Orbell 1998). The myth gives uncultivated food its permanent rank in the Māori order: kūmara and fernroot are the flesh of gods who would not fight, and every meal of them replays the ancient war.

myths.title: Aruhe, the Fernroot
myths.text: Haumia's living cult was the gathering of aruhe. From late winter into spring the people went out to the bracken clearings, dug the starchy rhizomes of the bracken fern with the foot-driven kō, and carried them home in baskets. The roots were beaten clean, washed in running water to leach the bitterness, and steamed for hours in the earth oven — hāngī, or umu tī, 'the fern oven'. When the kūmara crop failed, as it did in cold or wet years, aruhe carried whole communities through; Elsdon Best records that karakia were spoken over the digging, the cooking, and the first taste (Best, Māori Religion and Mythology). In Haumia's domain there is no sowing and no fence: only the earth's own stores, opened by labor and gratitude. The god of wild food teaches that plenty does not always need a garden — it needs a country loved enough to be read.

lore.syncretism: Within Polynesia, Haumia's closest relations are his own brothers. Rongo(-māui) — in Hawai'i Lono, in the Cook Islands Rongo — rules cultivated food and agriculture, and the two are sometimes treated as aspects of one god of vegetation; Margaret Orbell notes that in some recensions Haumia barely appears apart from Rongo. The wider Polynesian pattern is consistent: Tangaroa of the sea, Tāne of the forest, Rongo of the garden, Haumia of the wild ground. No Greco-Roman equivalent maps cleanly onto him — even Demeter presides over cultivated grain and never descends into the distinction the Māori make between what is planted and what is gathered. The most instructive comparison is structural: Haumia, like the Greek deities of the wildwood, sanctifies the food that lies outside the fence. In the modern revival of mātauranga Māori he has been recovered as the emblem of the uncultivated larder — the fern country that fed Aotearoa before agriculture and still feeds its imagination.
lore.culturalLegacy: Haumia's legacy is written into the New Zealand landscape and its food memory. Aruhe, fernroot, was the staple that carried Māori communities through winters and crop failures for centuries; the bracken clearings the digging parties made became, in places, the only open ground in the bush. The knowledge of gathering — where the fern grew thickest, how long to steam it — formed part of the mātauranga handed down within hapū, and it has returned in the modern revival of traditional foods and foraging. The digging stick (kō) he presided over survives in museum collections and in proverb: wild food is the food no one can fence, sell, or tax. Orbell's Concise Encyclopedia and Māori-medium teaching keep his name current, and the distinction he embodies — planted versus gathered — remains one of the most elegant classificatory ideas in any Polynesian pantheon.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Haumia-tiketike is the god of what the world gives freely and what we must still work to receive. The fernroot was never sown, never fenced, never owned — but it had to be found, dug, beaten, washed, and steamed for hours before it would feed anyone. His is the theology of uncultivated plenty: generosity without cultivation, labor without property. To meditate on Haumia is to ask where your own food comes from — not only the garden and the market but the ground itself, the wild margins, the places no deed encloses.

He is also the god who hid. While his brothers warred and were eaten or driven to sea, Haumia chose the earth-mother's body and stayed there, content to be the quiet portion of the world's food. In a pantheon of warriors and storm-gods, the gentle one survived by sheltering rather than fighting — and his reward was to become indispensable. The wild root outlasts the war.

lore.archaeology: No image or named shrine of Haumia survives — his was a cult of practice, not of temples. The material record is indirect but abundant: archaeobotanical studies of starch residues on prehistoric stone tools from sites across Aotearoa confirm that bracken fernroot was a dietary staple from the earliest settlement, and earth-oven (hāngī / umu tī) cooking features — fire-cracked stones in pits — are among the most common archaeological features on pre-European sites. Hardwood digging sticks (kō) survive in museum collections, their blades polished by generations of use. The archaeological signature of Haumia is, fittingly, everywhere and nowhere: not a temple to the god, but a landscape of fern country opened, dug, and steamed in his name.
